featureDeepDives.title: The Period Food Cost Percentage Formula
featureDeepDives.description: Period food cost measures your overall Cost of Goods Sold (COGS) relative to food revenue over a week, month, or quarter. It reflects real pantry consumption including waste and shrinkage.
bullets: Formula: Food Cost % = [(Beginning Inventory + Purchases - Ending Inventory) / Food Sales] × 100
Beginning Inventory: Total monetary value of raw ingredients at the start of the timeframe
Purchases: Total vendor invoices for food & beverage received during the timeframe
Ending Inventory: Total monetary value of physical stock remaining at period end

featureDeepDives.title: Dish / Plate-Level Recipe Costing
featureDeepDives.description: To price menu items profitably, you must calculate the portion cost of every single component on the plate (e.g. protein, sides, sauces, garnishes, and cooking oil).
bullets: Formula: Dish Food Cost % = (Total Raw Recipe Cost / Menu Selling Price) × 100
Target margin: Aim for 25% to 32% food cost on core entrees
Use high-margin appetizers and beverages (15% - 20%) to balance higher-cost premium proteins

featureDeepDives.title: Average Food Cost Benchmarks by Restaurant Concept
featureDeepDives.description: What is considered a 'healthy' food cost percentage depends entirely on your service model, menu complexity, and average check size.
bullets: Quick-Service (QSR) / Fast Food: 25% – 30% (High volume, standardized portions)
Fast Casual: 26% – 31% (Fresh ingredients, quick turnaround)
Full-Service Casual Dining: 28% – 34% (Diverse menu, scratch cooking)
Fine Dining: 30% – 36% (Premium cuts, intricate culinary labor)
Pizzerias & Pasta Houses: 18% – 25% (Low-cost flour and dough bases)

featureDeepDives.title: 5 Strategies Top Operators Use to Lower Food Cost
featureDeepDives.description: Lowering food costs by just 2% to 4% directly flows to your restaurant's bottom-line net profit. Here is how leading operators achieve sustainable savings:
bullets: Standardize portion control: Use portion scales, dedicated ladles, and prep recipe cards
Log daily kitchen waste: Track burnt dishes, dropped prep, and spoiled produce
Renegotiate with primary vendors: Consolidate orders to earn volume freight discounts
Automate recipe depletion: Connect POS sales to real-time inventory software

howItWorks.title: Determine Your Timeframe
howItWorks.description: Choose a consistent audit window (weekly or monthly). Run counts on the same day of the week (e.g., Sunday night after close).

howItWorks.title: Calculate Cost of Goods Sold (COGS)
howItWorks.description: Add Beginning Inventory to new purchases, then subtract your Ending Inventory count: COGS = Beg + Purchases - End.

howItWorks.title: Divide by Total Food Sales
howItWorks.description: Divide your total COGS by your gross food sales for that period, then multiply by 100 to get your Food Cost Percentage.

howItWorks.title: Compare Against Benchmarks & Optimize

faqs.question: What is food cost percentage?
faqs.answer: Food cost percentage is a critical restaurant financial metric that expresses the cost of raw ingredients as a percentage of the total revenue generated from selling those dishes. It reveals how efficiently your kitchen converts raw stock into profitable sales.

faqs.question: What is the formula for calculating food cost percentage?
faqs.answer: The period formula is: Food Cost % = [(Beginning Inventory + Purchases - Ending Inventory) / Total Food Sales] × 100. For an individual plate, the formula is: Dish Food Cost % = (Total Raw Recipe Cost / Menu Selling Price) × 100.

faqs.question: What is considered a good food cost percentage for a restaurant?
faqs.answer: For most full-service restaurants, a healthy food cost percentage falls between 28% and 32%. Pizzerias and cafes often achieve 20% to 25%, while steakhouses and seafood restaurants typically run between 32% and 36% due to high raw protein costs.

faqs.question: How often should a restaurant calculate its food cost percentage?
faqs.answer: Top operators calculate food cost weekly. Waiting for monthly or quarterly accounting reports makes it difficult to catch ingredient theft, vendor overcharges, or prep spoilage until thousands of dollars have already been lost.

faqs.question: What is the difference between ideal and actual food cost percentage?
faqs.answer: Ideal (theoretical) food cost is what your food cost should be based on your recipe portions and POS sales. Actual food cost is what you actually spent based on physical inventory. The difference between the two is called 'variance', representing waste, over-portioning, or theft.

faqs.question: How does automated restaurant software help control food cost?
faqs.answer: Automated software like SavoryOps tracks every gram of ingredient sold in real time, automatically alerts managers to inventory variances, highlights vendor price spikes, and calculates food cost percentages continuously without spreadsheets.

faqs.question: What is a KOT (Kitchen Order Ticket) in a restaurant?
faqs.answer: A Kitchen Order Ticket (KOT) is an operational document generated when an order is placed in a restaurant. It contains the table number, items ordered, quantity, preparation modifiers, and server name. It informs kitchen chefs what to prepare, in what sequence, and for which table.

faqs.question: What is the difference between KOT and BOT?
faqs.answer: KOT stands for Kitchen Order Ticket (routed to food preparation stations like the grill, fryer, or bakery), while BOT stands for Bar Order Ticket (routed specifically to the bartender for alcoholic beverages, mocktails, and specialty coffee drinks).

faqs.question: What is a Void KOT and why is it important?
faqs.answer: A Void KOT occurs when an item or entire ticket is cancelled after being sent to the kitchen. SavoryOps tracks Void KOTs with mandatory manager PIN authorization and reason codes, preventing food waste, employee theft, and revenue leakage.

faqs.question: Can SavoryOps print physical KOTs and also show digital kitchen screens?
faqs.answer: Yes. SavoryOps supports a hybrid workflow. You can print physical thermal KOTs at the kitchen pass while simultaneously displaying the digital orders on interactive kitchen display (KDS) tablets.

faqs.question: How does SavoryOps smart KOT prevent billing mistakes?
faqs.answer: Every generated KOT is permanently linked to the specific table session. When the guest requests the final bill, all items from multiple KOTs are automatically consolidated into one final invoice with zero missing items.

faqs.question: Can multiple KOTs be created for a single table?
faqs.answer: Yes. Guests often order starters first, followed by main courses and desserts later. SavoryOps allows unlimited incremental KOTs per table, keeping separate course numbers while combining them on the final receipt.
